item.research_question: Does non-random chemical mixing (short-range ordering) exist in CrCoNi medium-entropy alloys, and how does it vary with thermomechanical history and influence dislocation slip behavior?
item.material_system: CrCoNi medium-entropy alloy (equiatomic Cr, Co, Ni)
item.processing_route: Arc melting and drop casting (5x repetition) followed by homogenization at 1200 °C for 48 h; one sample water-quenched (WQ), the other aged at 1000 °C for 120 h followed by furnace cooling (HT)
item.test_conditions: Room temperature tensile testing at a strain rate of 1 × 10−3 s−1; electron nanodiffraction (SEND) with 1.1 mrad semi-convergence angle and 10 eV energy filter; Small-Angle Neutron Scattering (SANS); Atom Probe Tomography (APT) at 50 K base temperature
key_findings: Two types of short-range order (SRO) were identified: L12 (minimizing Cr–Cr nearest neighbors) and L11 (segregating Cr on alternating close-packed planes).
In the water-quenched (WQ) sample, L11-type nanoclusters are predominant, whereas in the heat-treated (HT) sample, L12-type nanoclusters become more dominant.
The L12-type diffuse peaks are split, a feature consistent with Fermi surface nesting mechanisms observed in binary alloys like CuPd.
Estimated SRO parameters for L12 ordering are α_CrCo = α_CrNi = −0.18, consistent with Monte-Carlo DFT theory predictions.
Dislocation slip behavior changes drastically: WQ shows wavy dislocations mixed with localized planar slips, while HT exhibits extensive planar slips with paired dislocations.
SANS detected scattering objects with a Guinier radius of gyration Rg ~ 3.0 Å in both samples, indicating sub-nm chemical fluctuations.
APT analysis revealed Ni-rich and Cr-poor nanoclusters of a few nm in size with negative Ni-Cr and Co-Cr correlations.
Yield strengths were similar for both samples (227 MPa for WQ and 224 MPa for HT), attributed to the presence of CSRO in both.
item.mechanism: The L12-type ordering is driven by magnetic interactions (minimizing Cr–Cr pairs in favor of Cr–Co/Cr–Ni) and Fermi surface instability, while L11-type ordering involves segregation on alternating {111} planes. The destruction of L12-type CSRO by leading dislocations creates diffuse antiphase boundaries with higher energy, causing paired dislocations to form to reduce energy costs, resulting in a glide plane softening effect and extensive planar slip.
item.limitations: The study notes that neither the L11 nor L12 CSRO models explain the (3̄11)/2 diffuse spot observed in cold-rolled samples by previous researchers, indicating multiplicity of local bonding preferences dependent on history. Additionally, standard atomic-resolution STEM imaging showed no obvious evidence of CSRO, highlighting the need for the developed data-driven approach.
item.future_work: The authors suggest the methodology provides general opportunities for atomistic-structure study in concentrated alloys for the design of strong and ductile materials, and imply further investigation into the specific role of magnetic interactions and Fermi surface instabilities in driving CSRO.
quotes: Two samples, one homogenized and one heat-treated, are observed. In both samples, results reveal two types of short-range-order inside nanoclusters that minimize the Cr–Cr nearest neighbors (L12) or segregate Cr on alternating close-packed planes (L11).
The L11 is predominant in the homogenized sample, while the L12 formation is promoted by heat-treatment, with the latter being accompanied by a dramatic change in dislocation-slip behavior.
The formation of PDs is due to the destruction of the L12-type CSRO by the leading dislocation, which creates higher energy at the diffuse antiphase boundary.
